pamphlet_excerpts: Need for Bird Study: Birds lend life, color, and music to the outdoors, and they are an important part of the ecosystems that keep this planet healthy (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 2: Because they are sensitive to changes in the environment, birds are valuable indicators of trouble, including pollution and habitat loss (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 3: It was the near-disappearance of bald eagles, peregrine falcons, and brown pelicans decades ago that alerted people to the dangers of many (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 4: Major, rapid declines in the number of songbirds have shown that we must preserve large areas for wildlife habitat (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Need for Bird Study): Each species is lumped with its closest relatives to form a genus, usually on the basis of physical characteristics like the shapes of certain bones (p. 10).
Step 2 (Need for Bird Study): Closely related genera (the plural of "genus") are grouped together to form a family (p. 10).
Step 3 (Need for Bird Study): Most field guides are arranged in this taxonomic order (p. 10).
Step 4 (Need for Bird Study): Because related birds often act and look somewhat the same, knowing these relationships can help you identify a new, puzzling species (p. 10).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Bird Study Requirement 1, why do ecologists regard wild bird populations as vital bioindicators of environmental health?
quiz_item.question: In Bird Study Requirement 1, why do ecologists regard wild bird populations as vital bioindicators of environmental health?
options: A. Because birds never migrate outside a single square mile, making them immune to weather or habitat changes elsewhere.
B. Because birds feed exclusively on inorganic soil minerals and are unaffected by agricultural pesticides or wetland loss.

C. Because birds occupy diverse trophic levels, respond rapidly to habitat fragmentation, insect declines, and chemical pollutants (such as DDT thinning eggshells), and perform critical seed dispersal and pest control.
D. Because wild birds can survive indefinitely in polluted industrial zones without clean water or native plant cover.
choices: A. Because birds never migrate outside a single square mile, making them immune to weather or habitat changes elsewhere.
B. Because birds feed exclusively on inorganic soil minerals and are unaffected by agricultural pesticides or wetland loss.

C. Because birds occupy diverse trophic levels, respond rapidly to habitat fragmentation, insect declines, and chemical pollutants (such as DDT thinning eggshells), and perform critical seed dispersal and pest control.
D. Because wild birds can survive indefinitely in polluted industrial zones without clean water or native plant cover.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because birds occupy diverse trophic levels, respond rapidly to habitat fragmentation, insect declines, and chemical pollutants (such as DDT thinning eggshells), and perform critical seed dispersal and pest control.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Birds are sensitive to changes in insect abundance, water quality, climate, and chemical contaminants across ecosystems, making population trends a reliable early warning of environmental stress.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Go on a field trip with a local club or with others who are knowledgeable about birds in your area. (1) Keep a list or fill out a checklist of all the birds your group observed during the field trip. (2) Tell your counselor which birds your group saw and why some species were common and some were present in small numbers. (3) Tell your counselor what makes the area you visited good for finding birds. (b) By using a public library, the internet, or contacting the National Audubon Society, find the name and location of the Christmas Bird Count nearest your home and obtain the results of a recent count. (1) Explain what kinds of information are collected during the annual event. (2) Tell your counselor which species are most common, and explain why these birds are abundant. (3) Tell your counselor which species are uncommon, and explain why these were present in small numbers. If the number of birds of these species is decreasing, explain why, and what, if anything, could be done to reverse their decline. (c) Participate in a bird banding program with an approved federal or state agency, university researcher, bird observatory, or certified private individual. (1) Explain who is able to band birds and why. (2) Explain why birds get banded. (3) Explain what kinds of birds get banded. (4) Tell how the birds were captured, the number of bird species recorded during your visit, and your role in the program.
